domains.label: Legal & Compliance
domains.rationale: The talk centers on multi-agent system design for legal workflows, covering agent decomposition, accuracy chaining, guardrails, episodic memory, and human-in-the-loop controls. The entire presentation concerns legal litigation—class action and mass tort case research, discovery, and lead qualification for law firms. The speaker discusses both building multi-agent systems and operating production agents with daily graph construction and iterative pruning. Prerequisites include familiarity with graph databases, multi-agent architectures, and legal discovery processes. This is a technical conference presentation on the AI Engineer YouTube channel by a technical founder. All evidence anchors are sourced directly from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Tom Smoker, technical founder of WhyHow.ai, presents on applying knowledge graphs and multi-agent systems to legal litigation, focusing on class action and mass tort cases. WhyHow finds cases before law firms do by scraping the entire web, qualifying leads through firm-specific schemas, and generating personalized reports—all automated end-to-end. Smoker has worked with graphs for about a decade and was previously an academic in multi-agent systems. He defines graphs fundamentally as relations enabling visual inspection, explicit connection specification including multihop traversals, and large-scale analytics. For discovery, graphs transform mountains of irrelevant documents into structured form where experts can visually and via natural language hone in on what matters—e.g., in pharmaceutical cases, identifying the few problematic nodes among millions. They have agents in production enabling lawyers to query lawsuits and represented individuals in natural language. For case research, people complain about products on forums, subreddits, and government websites using similar language; WhyHow scrapes, structures, schematizes, and analyzes this data to build complaint density (complaint count × velocity) for specific vehicles, years, and problems. In a car-fire case study, they found actionable signals in about 15 minutes and confirmed confidence within a month, versus 8–9 months for large law firms. Each lawyer receives a different multi-agent system and graph matching their specific workflow, with reports sharing consistent structure but personalized content. Graphs are built daily as a monolithic structure from which subgraphs are composed into actionable reports. Smoker stresses that GenAI is not better than traditional ML; rather, LLMs allow piping together previously disconnected ML-filtered systems, enabling complete end-to-end value delivery. Iterative graph building and pruning improves reports over time through managed state. The legal domain demands near-perfect accuracy plus creative reasoning (exemplified by applying Blockbuster's DVD-tracking precedent to Netflix's data collection), creating friction with probabilistic LLMs. Five 95%-accurate agents chained yield only 77% combined accuracy, framing the core challenge as decision-making under uncertainty, mitigated through guardrails, episodic memory, and human-in-the-loop controls.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Tom Smoker introduces himself as technical founder of WhyHow.ai, which finds class action and mass tort cases before lawyers do using graphs, multi-agent systems, signals, and web scraping. He outlines the schema emerging from legal domain entities: individuals, products, ingredients, concentrations, and ID numbers.

sections.title: Defining Graphs and Their Challenges
sections.summary: Defines graphs as relations enabling visual inspection, explicit connection specification, and large-scale analytics including multihop traversals. Discusses the difficulty that people use graph terminology inconsistently, making definitions important when building production systems.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Systems in Legal Workflows
sections.summary: Explains how multi-agent systems decompose complex legal workflows into specific testable steps with different requirements, frequencies, and state. Lawyers demand correctness, so probabilistic LLMs alone are insufficient—structured control, schema, and testability are required.

sections.title: Accuracy Challenges and Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
sections.summary: Discusses issues with multi-agent systems: uneven workflow importance, bad prompts producing bad agents, few trustworthy agents. They use guardrails, episodic memory, and state pruning in graphical format. Five 95%-accurate agents chained yield only 77% combined accuracy, framing the core problem as decision-making under uncertainty.

sections.title: Legal Industry Context: Accuracy Plus Creativity
sections.summary: Legal work requires perfect accuracy plus creative argumentation. The Netflix data-collection case drawing precedent from Blockbuster's DVD-tracking lawsuit illustrates creative legal reasoning from latent expert knowledge. Probabilistic agents frustrate lawyers when they are creatively wrong.

sections.title: Legal Discovery and Graph-Based Structuring
sections.summary: Legal discovery involves opponents dumping hundreds of gigabytes of largely irrelevant documents. Currently manually reviewed under tight timelines, graphs can extract and structure this information consistently, separating dismissible noise from genuinely useful information and enabling augmentation of discovery findings.

sections.title: Graph-Based Discovery: Visual and Natural-Language Decision-Making
sections.summary: Returns to the pharmaceutical example: graphs with millions of nodes contain only a few problematic people, mirroring the few relevant documents in discovery. Graphs change the form factor so experts can hone in visually and via natural language, enabling data-driven decisions. Production agents allow lawyers to query lawsuits and represented individuals in natural language via graph RAG.

sections.title: Case Research: From Web Scraping to Qualified Personalized Leads
sections.summary: Case research involves people complaining about products online—on subreddits, Twitter, forums, IRC—using similar language. WhyHow scrapes the entire web, then qualifies leads through schemas specific to each law firm and lawyer. No perfect case exists; matching is about specificity and personalization. Different lawyers get different multi-agent systems and graphs matching their workflow. Reports share consistent structure but personalized content per lawyer.

sections.title: Car-Fire Case Study: Complaint Density and Early Signal Detection
sections.summary: People whose cars catch fire complain on government websites, carcomplaints.com, subreddits, and forums. WhyHow scrapes, structures, schematizes, and analyzes to build complaint density (complaint count × velocity) per vehicle, year, and problem. They find actionable signals in about 15 minutes and reach confidence within a month, versus 8–9 months for large law firms. Lawyer-specific filters (money, make/model, jurisdiction) are applied as schema throughout the graph.

sections.title: Report Generation and Extensible Graph Schema
sections.summary: Graphs are built daily as monolithic structures; subgraphs are composed into actionable lawyer reports. The interface is less chat-RAG and more report generation, giving lawyers the form factor they expect. Graphs are extensible schemas—updatable, queryable, and not static. Each lawyer's graph and multi-agent system match their specific process.

sections.title: Future: LLMs Piping Together ML-Filtered Systems
sections.summary: Smoker stresses GenAI is not better than traditional ML, but LLMs excel at piping together previously disconnected ML-filtered systems, enabling end-to-end value delivery that was previously impossible. Iterative graph building and pruning with managed state improves reports over time. WhyHow's value proposition is consistent tracking of exactly what each lawyer specifically wants.
